learning_outcomes: Explain the role of reusable html and layouts in a Classic ASP application.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study reusable html and layouts as part of Classic ASP development and legacy maintenance. The lesson follows the attached ASP curriculum topic 39 and uses the syllabus subtopics as the coverage checklist.
content.why_it_matters: Reusable HTML and Layouts matters because Classic ASP behavior crosses a server-side scripting engine, IIS configuration, request/response boundaries, and often COM or ADO dependencies. A small, explicit test helps distinguish intended behavior from runtime-specific behavior.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Classic ASP templates mix HTML output and server-side script. In 'Reusable HTML and Layouts', keep presentation readable while ensuring every dynamic value is encoded for its output context. Server-side checks are authoritative; client-side JavaScript can improve usability but cannot enforce access, validate trusted data, or protect database operations.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus coverage
content_blocks.text: The lesson explicitly covers: Shared navigation and headers; Shared footers; Content areas and page composition; Dynamic navigation; Consistent page layouts; Avoiding deeply nested script and markup blocks. Treat these subtopics as connected requirements. For each one, be able to define the concept, identify where it appears in a Classic ASP application, and name one test or diagnostic that would verify it.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Submit requests through a browser to a local/test IIS site. Test missing fields, repeated parameters, session expiry, and a second request; do not infer security from a successful happy path. The source syllabus treats Classic ASP as a legacy maintenance technology, not as ASP.NET or a default choice for new web projects.

content_blocks.title: Guided workflow
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with a minimal local example of reusable html and layouts. 2. Trace its inputs, state changes, dependencies, and output. 3. Test a normal case, a missing/malformed case, and one permission/provider/runtime failure. 4. Write down the exact expected and observed result before changing another variable.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating legacy runtime behavior as universal.
common_mistakes.why: IIS versions, Windows lifecycle, COM registration/bitness, and ADO providers can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the actual server/provider versions and validate on a disposable test site.

common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing records, expired sessions, permissions, timeouts, and malformed data reveal different failure modes.
common_mistakes.fix: Add normal, negative, and boundary cases with expected outcomes.

common_mistakes.why: Detailed errors can reveal paths, SQL text, configuration, and component information.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep diagnostics in restricted server-side logs and return a generic message with a reference ID.
